translations.text: Then King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, wise and great-minded, honouring those words spoken by Vidura, asked Sanatsujāta, in a secluded place, about the highest understanding, wishing to become (his own Self again).

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the text: after a verse of homage to Viṣṇu, the ancient Puruṣa, full bliss, cause of the universe, and homage to the teachers who handed down the knowledge of Brahman, he begins a short explanation of the Sanatsujātīya, for the easy understanding of those who wish to know Brahman. The Self, though by nature Brahman — consciousness, being, bliss, without a second — through its own ignorance, which rests on it, has it for its object, is known in its own experience and carries a reflection (of consciousness), falls from that natural being as Brahman and takes the not-self, the body and the rest, as itself. Every human end then escapes it and every evil comes to it; it seeks the wanted and avoids the unwanted by means that ignorance and action have imagined, and even by worldly and Vedic means duly performed it does not gain the highest end, called liberation. Dragged here and there by passion, aversion and the like, as by sea-monsters, it turns about in many births, among gods, men, animals and the rest, deluded, in saṃsāra. Then somehow, by merit, through action done for the Lord as the Veda enjoins, the stain of passion and the rest goes; from seeing the faults of impermanence and the like, dispassion arises for enjoying fruits here and hereafter; wishing to know the oneness with Brahman that the Vedānta teaches, and having calm, self-restraint and the other means the Veda names, he approaches a teacher who knows Brahman, and by hearing the Vedānta and the rest, as the teacher directs, he knows the truth of the Self as Brahman, ‘I am Brahman’; ignorance and its effects ended, he abides as Brahman. ‘This is the bound of the Vedānta’; the blessed Sanatsujāta will show all of it in order.

Śaṅkara, on the setting: Dhṛtarāṣṭra, burning with grief and delusion, had heard the Vedānta's word ‘the knower of the Self crosses over grief’ (Chāndogya 7.1.3) and, thinking grief cannot be removed without the knowledge of Brahman, asked Vidura to tell him anything he had not yet told. Vidura, though he had heard the teaching, all-knowing and most compassionate, held that the knowledge of Brahman belongs to those specially qualified, and said ‘Born of a śūdra womb, I do not venture to say more’, that is, he was not entitled to the Upaniṣadic knowledge of the Self as Brahman. Wishing all the same to establish the king, by that knowledge, in the supreme state, the Supreme Self, full bliss, his own kingdom, he remembered the story known from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (Sanatkumāra's teaching of the bhūman), thought that no one but Sanatsujāta could show the king the Supreme Self beyond darkness, called him by the power of yoga, honoured him by rising to meet him and the like, and asked him to resolve the doubt in Dhṛtarāṣṭra's mind, so that, hearing him, the king would pass beyond all sorrow, bear gain and loss, the loved and the hated, old age and death, intoxication, hunger and thirst, fear, discontent, sloth, desire and anger, decline and rise, and be freed from dharma and adharma, the causes of saṃsāra, liberated, beyond pleasure and pain.

Śaṅkara: tat vākyam: the words Vidura spoke to Sanatsujāta just before. Sanatsujāta: ‘sanat’ is the eternal Brahman called Hiraṇyagarbha; born well (sujāta), with knowledge, dispassion and the rest, from that eternal Brahman's mind, he is the blessed Sanatkumāra. rahite: in a secluded place, free of common people. mahātmā: of great understanding. buddhiṃ paramām: the highest understanding, whose object is the full bliss without a second. bubhūṣan: wishing to become, that is, wishing to gain, by the knowledge of Brahman, the Self that had been taken from him.

translations.text: O Sanatsujāta, I hear this teaching of yours, that there is no death; (yet) the gods and asuras lived the life of a brahmacārin for deathlessness. Of these, which then is true?

notes: Śaṅkara: Vidura says that you taught your disciples ‘there is no death’; yet the gods and asuras, Indra, Virocana and the rest, lived the life of a brahmacārin, dwelling with the teacher, for deathlessness, to gain deathlessness, as the Chāndogya tells: ‘both the gods and the asuras came to know of it’, ‘the two lived as brahmacārins for thirty-two years’ (8.7.2–3), and ‘Maghavan lived with Prajāpati as a brahmacārin for a hundred and one years’ (8.11.3). If your view is that there is no death, why did the gods and asuras live so for deathlessness? Of the two views, that death is and that it is not, tell which is true.

translations.text: Some (say) deathlessness (comes) by action; others, that there is no death. Hear me, O king, as I tell how this (stands); do not doubt (what I say).

notes: Śaṅkara: some, set in ignorance and holding death to be real, think deathlessness comes by the action the Veda enjoins, and perform it for deathlessness. Others, blinded by the poison of sense-objects and not admitting a liberation without objects, describe deathlessness as reaching the state of a god and the like by action alone, and quote a passionate man's verse: ‘Let him rather wish to be a jackal in the empty Vṛndāvana, but never an objectless liberation, Gautama.’ Others again, seeing a second beside the Supreme Self, describe deathlessness as coming from knowledge and action together. Others still, who see the Self without a second, see nothing second to it and say ‘there is no death’. Hear from me, O king, how the two views do not conflict; mā viśaṅkithāḥ: have no doubt about what I say.

translations.text: Both are true, O warrior, current from the first (creation). Delusion is held to be death by (some) sages; but I call heedlessness death, and constant heedfulness I call deathlessness.

notes: The edition prints kṣatriyādyapravṛtte as one word; Śaṅkara divides it as kṣatriya (vocative) and ādyapravṛtte, or, second, as kṣatriyādya (vocative, ‘first of warriors’) and pravṛtte (‘current’).

Śaṅkara: ubhe: both, the being and the not-being of death spoken of before; ādyapravṛtte: current since the first creation. How can two contradictory things both be true? There would be a contradiction if death were something real. What then is death? Delusion, false knowledge, the taking of the not-self as self, is held to be death by some sages; I do not call death that. I call heedlessness death: pramāda is the falling away from one's natural being as Brahman; that heedlessness, the failure to grasp the Self, ignorance of the Self, the cause even of false knowledge, the seed of every evil, birth, death and the rest, I call death. Constant heedfulness, abiding in one's own nature, I call deathlessness. So the śruti shows liberation to be abiding in one's own nature: ‘having reached the highest light, he appears in his own form’ (Chāndogya 8.3.4); and the Anugītā says it plainly: there is one sacrifice, no second, the one that lies in the heart, in whom mortals, having swallowed all this, stand in their own nature.

Śaṅkara: since liberation is abiding in one's own nature, and so unlike the four kinds of result an act can have, deathlessness is not produced by action, nor by knowledge and action together; the view ‘some (say) deathlessness (comes) by action’ (verse 3) is therefore untenable. Sanatsujāta himself refutes it below, in verse 9 (Śaṅkara quotes it with a second half: by knowledge the knower goes to the eternal light; for him there is no other path).

translations.text: Through heedlessness the asuras were defeated, and through heedfulness the gods became Brahman. Death does not eat creatures like a tiger; for its form is not even perceived.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the verse: how is it known that heedlessness is death and heedfulness deathlessness?

Śaṅkara: through heedlessness, the falling away from one's natural being as Brahman and taking the not-self, the body and the rest, as self, the asuras, Virocana and the others, were defeated, as the Chāndogya tells from ‘not having found the Self’ to ‘they will be defeated’ (8.8.4). Through heedfulness, abiding as Brahman, consciousness, being, bliss without a second, the gods, Indra and the rest, became Brahman: ‘the gods worship that Self; therefore all worlds and all desires are theirs’ (Chāndogya 8.12.6). Or: asuras are those who delight in the asus, the breaths and the senses: creatures who do not know the Self and live for objects. Going beyond their natural being as Brahman and taking the body as self, they were defeated, falling into animal and other births, as the Aitareya Āraṇyaka says from ‘therefore let one not be heedless’ to ‘those three peoples that went beyond became these birds …’ (2.1.1). And suras are those who delight in their own Self, the knowers of the Self: ‘those whose delight is in the Self, in their own unmoving Brahman, are called suras; the wise (sūri) are held to be suras.’ Through heedfulness, abiding as Brahman, false knowledge and its effects ended, they became Brahman itself.

Śaṅkara, on the second half: the objection is that another death, the destroyer of all creatures, is well known; how then can heedlessness be called death? He answers: death does not eat creatures like a tiger; if it did, its form would be perceived like a tiger's; it is not perceived; so there is no (such) death.

words.meaning: in the world of the fathers

translations.text: But some call Yama death, other than this (heedlessness): dwelling in the self (the intellect), deathless, established in Brahman. The god rules a kingdom in the world of the fathers, kind to the good, unkind to the wicked.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the verse: but Yama's form is perceived, in the story of Sāvitrī: ‘Then from Satyavān's body Yama drew out by force the thumb-sized person, bound by the noose, in his power.’ How then is it said that death's form is not perceived?

Śaṅkara: it is true that (Yama's form) is perceived; yet he is not death directly. Death is the ignorance called heedlessness, for it is the direct cause of destruction: ‘if one has not known here, great is the loss’ (Kena 2.5); and the Bṛhadāraṇyaka shows that the ignorance called heedlessness is death itself: ‘death is darkness, light is the deathless’ (1.3.28). Since heedlessness is the direct seed of every evil, let one not be heedless: let one abide as Brahman, consciousness, being, bliss without a second (Gītā 5.15: knowledge is covered by ignorance, by that creatures are deluded). Then ‘by the way’ he sets out the meaning of the whole śāstra in brief, as outlined in the next six notes.

Śaṅkara (1), knowledge alone liberates: since heedlessness is death and heedfulness deathlessness, deathlessness is neither produced nor reached by action, being ever accomplished and ever attained (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.23: this eternal greatness of the brāhmaṇa neither grows nor lessens by action). Knowledge alone is the means: ‘knowing him alone one goes beyond death; there is no other path’ (Śvetāśvatara 3.8), ‘knowing him alone, let the wise brāhmaṇa make wisdom’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.21), ‘not by the eye … not by austerity or action; by the clearness of knowledge, pure in mind, he sees him’ (Muṇḍaka 3.1.8). Sanatsujāta says the same below (the worlds won by action end; ‘knowing death thus as it arises’, verse 16); so the Mokṣadharma (a creature is bound by action, freed by knowledge; so the renouncers who see the far shore do no action; knowledge, not sacrifice, crosses the hard way); Manu (12.92: leaving even the prescribed actions, the best of the twice-born should strive in Self-knowledge, calm and the study of the Veda); and the Supreme Lord (knowledge alone gives liberation; the one Self, all-pervading, pure consciousness, bliss, is to be known — ‘this is the Sāṃkhya view’; the renouncers devoted to it reach me).

Śaṅkara (2), actions are not for the knower: are actions then not to be done? Not so; they are not to be done by the knower: ‘for him who delights in the Self alone … there is nothing to be done’ (Gītā 3.17); the Kāvaṣeyas in the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa (what is study to us, why should we sacrifice; we offer prāṇa in speech and speech in prāṇa); the Aitareya (‘for what shall we study?’); the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, which shows the knower's renunciation of action (4.4.22: the knowers of old, rising above the desire for sons, for wealth and for the worlds, lived as mendicants); the Liṅga Purāṇa (for the yogin content with the nectar of knowledge nothing remains to be done; if anything does, he is not a knower of the truth); an Ātharvaṇa śruti. By whom then? By the ignorant who wish to ascend, all actions always; not by the knower (Gītā 3.3, 6.3; Vyāsa: there are two paths on which the Vedas rest, dharma marked by activity and dharma that stands in withdrawal).

Śaṅkara (3), actions purify, they do not liberate: if action binds, should even those who wish to ascend not act? True, it binds; yet done for the Lord, without regard to the fruit, it does not (Gītā 3.9); it is done for the purity of the mind (Gītā 5.11, 18.5, 4.23; ‘actions ripen the impurities; knowledge is the highest goal’). Objection: the śruti makes action a cause of liberation too (Īśa 11 and 2; Manu: ‘austerity and knowledge both bring the brāhmaṇa the highest good’). No: that error comes from not reading what goes before and after. Īśa 11 goes on: ‘by ignorance crossing death, by knowledge one gains the deathless’, so the two have different objects and are not combined; Manu himself explains: ‘by austerity he destroys sin, by knowledge gains the deathless’, so austerity, the obligatory and occasional rites, serves only the purity of the inner organ. Īśa 1 says all this is (the Lord) and enjoins protecting oneself by renunciation for one who sees it; for one who does not know that Self, Īśa 2 says ‘doing works here, let one wish to live a hundred years’: works lifelong, for the purity of the ignorant man who thinks himself a mere man. So these texts too teach purification, not liberation; and the ‘and’ of ‘by it goes the knower of Brahman, the doer of merit and the luminous’ (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.9) is to be construed by the established use of the śruti. The Anugītā says plainly that actions lead to liberation only through purity: by obligatory and occasional rites, pure and without attachment to fruit, one gains purity of mind, ascends to yoga, and reaches the highest place of Viṣṇu; spotless knowledge arises from devotion to the teacher, firmness, devotion to dharma, learning and devotion to Viṣṇu. Sanatsujāta too says it (adhyāya 2: by austerity and sacrifice the knower gains merit; by merit destroying sin he is born lit by knowledge; by knowledge he reaches the Self).

Śaṅkara (4), why purity is needed: liberation comes by knowledge alone, even without purity? True, liberation is by knowledge alone; but that knowledge does not arise without purity of mind: ‘knowledge arises in men from the wearing away of sinful action’; while the heap of sin gathered in many births is not worn away, the mind does not turn to Govinda; devotion to Kṛṣṇa arises in those whose sins are worn away by austerity, meditation and absorption over thousands of births; Gītā 6.45, 6.46, 18.45–46; Yājñavalkya: one whose instrument is unripe is not fit for Self-knowledge. Since knowledge, the means of liberation, comes only to the pure in mind, through discerning the eternal from the transient, one should do all actions, of speech, mind and body, enjoined by śruti and smṛti, for the Lord of all, until, pure in mind and without desire for enjoyment here or hereafter, one has ascended to yoga (Gītā 6.3, 5.6, 6.4); for him who has so ascended, calm alone is the means, not action.

Śaṅkara (5), the practice: so, with calm, self-restraint and the other means, with hearing and the rest, ‘the yogin should constantly join himself, alone, in a secluded place’ (Gītā 6.10). How? On a level, clean place pleasing to the mind, free of gravel, fire, sand, noise, water and the like, setting a firm seat neither too high nor too low, of cloth, skin and kuśa grass, seated in the svastika or the lotus posture, holding body, head and neck straight, withdrawing Viśva and the rest in order into the full Self free of effect and cause, abiding as the full Self, he should meditate, as Om, on the deity dwelling in the body, full bliss, stainless, Brahman without before or after, marked by ‘not this, not this’, untouched by hunger and the rest, abiding as knowledge that neither rises nor sets: the Supreme Self (the Kāvaṣeya-gītā: strive for liberation; take to Om, Brahman, the void, the highest, the chief, pure bliss, the praṇava). When, so joining himself, he knows himself directly as the Supreme Self, ignorance and its effects are cast off, he is free of sorrow, his work done (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.12; Īśa 7; Kaṭha 1.2.12, 1.3.15; Taittirīya 2.9; Muṇḍaka 2.2.8; Gītā 2.25, 15.20; the Kāvaṣeya-gītā: he is not born, does not die, is neither bound nor freed; when the noose of ignorance is broken and the seeds of birth are burnt he goes to the highest bliss; Manu 12.85, 12.93). Since the highest end comes from that knowledge alone, one should know the Supreme Self, full bliss, as oneself, ‘I am (he)’, and think of nothing else (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.21; Muṇḍaka 2.2.5; Śvetāśvatara 1.12; Gītā 6.24–25). ‘So, by the way, the meaning of the whole śāstra has been shown in brief.’

Śaṅkara (6), on the verse itself: since heedlessness alone is the seed of every evil, I call heedlessness death, not Yama. But some, blinded by the poison of objects, set in ignorance, seeing a second beside their own Self, call another than the death called heedlessness, Vaivasvata, death. ātmāvāsam: he who dwells in the self, in the intellect (Manu 8.92: Yama Vaivasvata, the king who stands in your heart). amṛtam: not subject to death. brahmacaryam: moving, delighting, in Brahman, his own Self; established in Brahman (Kaṭha 1.2.21: who but I can know that god, rejoicing and not rejoicing?). Further, the god rules a kingdom in the world of the fathers: śivaḥ, giving happiness, to the śivas, those of good deeds; aśivaḥ, giving unhappiness, to the aśivas, those of evil deeds.
The edition: the transcript marks mṛtyum ato as doubtful in the print (the letter after ‘m’ looks like ‘n’); the reading ato is kept.

आस्यादेष निःसरते नराणां क्रोधः प्रमादो मोहरूपश्च मृत्युः ।
अहंगतेनैव चरन्विमार्गान्न चात्मनो योगमुपैति किंचित् ॥ ७ ॥

ahaṃgatenaiva caran vimārgān na cātmano yogam upaiti kiṃcit || 7 ||

grammar.en: past passive participle n. ins. sg.

translations.text: From the mouth (the sense of ‘I’) this death goes forth in men, as anger, as heedlessness and in the form of delusion. Going in wrong ways through (ignorance) become ‘I’, he does not reach union with the Self at all.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the verse: so far the nature of death has been settled by ‘I call heedlessness death’; now he shows it standing as its effects.

Śaṅkara: this death of ignorance called heedlessness first turns into the ‘mouth’: āsya is the sense of ‘I’ (ahaṃkāra), whose nature is pride (a verse: the dreadful ahaṃkāra, a great guṇa, is called āsya, because it gathers in all objects and is joined with the root as). Standing as the sense of ‘I’, it goes forth from it as desire; desire, moving toward its objects and checked, becomes anger, heedlessness and delusion. Then, through the ignorance become ‘I’, standing as the sense of ‘I’ and the rest, a man takes himself to be that — ‘I am a brāhmaṇa, I am a kṣatriya, I am lean, I am stout, the son of so-and-so, the grandson of this one’ — and, with passion, aversion and the rest, going in wrong ways contrary to śruti and smṛti, he does not reach even a little the union (yoga) with the Self, the Supreme Self, which is absorption (samādhi).

Śaṅkara, second explanation: ignorance, desire and action set saṃsāra going. Ignorance, the not grasping and the wrong grasping (of the Self), was named in ‘delusion is held to be death’ (verse 4); action will be named in ‘when action arises’ (verse 9); here desire is named: āsya is desire, because by it creatures are cast (as) into saṃsāra, or it is a mouth because it devours everything (Gītā 3.37: it is desire, it is anger). This death, standing as desire, turns into anger (Gītā 2.62: from desire anger is born); then, through ignorance become ‘I’ — the reflection of consciousness mounted on the board of ‘I’ and ‘mine’ — going in wrong ways, he does not reach union with the Self at all.

sanskrit.deva:

past passive participle m. nom. pl.

translations.text: Deluded (by it), living in its power, they depart from here and, (having stayed) there, fall again. Then the gods (the senses) float about after him; therefore he (goes) to death, and from dying he goes on (to another birth).

notes: Śaṅkara: deluded by that ignorance turned into the sense of ‘I’ and the rest, made to take the body and the rest as self, living in the power of the death called heedlessness so turned, they depart from here by the path of smoke and the rest, stay there in the other world until (their merit) is spent, and fall again, by way of space, wind, rain, grain, food, semen and blood, to take a body: ‘having stayed there until it is spent, they return by the same way’ (Chāndogya 5.10.5). Then, when he takes a body, the gods, the senses, following his actions, float all about him: they circle all round. Therefore, from following the qualities of the senses, he goes to death, dying; from dying he goes on to another birth, and from it to death again. So, mounted on the chain of births and deaths, he is never freed. Since saṃsāra has ignorance of the Self for its cause, as long as he does not directly know the Supreme Self as himself he remains in saṃsāra, overcome by the three afflictions, dragged here and there by passion and the rest as by sea-monsters, ever more deluded.

सदर्थयोगानवगमात्समन्तात्प्रवर्तते भोगयोगेन देही ॥ ९ ॥

padaccheda.deva: कर्म-उदये कर्म-फल-अनुरागाः तत्र अनुयान्ति न तरन्ति मृत्युम् सत्-अर्थ-योग-अनवगमात् समन्तात् प्रवर्तते भोग-योगेन देही

words.meaning: attached to the fruits of action
from not knowing union with the real

translations.text: When action arises, attached to the fruits of action, they follow there; they do not cross death. From not knowing union with the Real (the Supreme Self), the embodied one goes on, on every side, by union with enjoyment.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the verse: so far ignorance and desire have been shown to be causes of bondage; now he shows that actions are too.

Śaṅkara: this refutes the other view set out in verse 3, that deathlessness comes by action. Not only does deathlessness not come by action: when actions arise, men attached to their fruits follow there, into that fruit; since they follow there, they do not cross death: they turn again and again in saṃsāra, which is birth and death. Why? sadarthayogānavagamāt: sadarthayoga is union with the Real, with the Supreme Self, oneness; from not knowing it, that is, from not knowing one's own Self as Brahman, consciousness and bliss without a second, the embodied one goes on everywhere by union with enjoyment, with the thought that objects have savour. As a blind man wanders over low and high ground and thorny places, so he, without discernment, wanders everywhere in longing for the pleasure of objects.

The edition: the transcript marks tatrānuyānti as doubtful in the print (the first letters of the line are smeared). Śaṅkara, quoting the verse in his comment on verse 4, reads karmaphalānurāgāt tatrānuyānti; his gloss here (karmaphalānurāgāḥ santaḥ) follows the reading printed.

मिथ्यार्थयोगाभिहतान्तरात्मा स्मरन्नुपास्ते विषयान्समन्तात् ॥ १० ॥

mithyārthayogābhihatāntarātmā smarann upāste viṣayān samantāt || 10 ||

mithyārthayogābhihatāntarātmā smarann upāste viṣayān samantāt

padaccheda.iast: tat vai mahā-mohanam indriyāṇām mithyā-artha-yoge asya gatiḥ hi nityā mithyā-artha-yoga-abhihata-antarātmā smaran upāste viṣayān samantāt
padaccheda.deva: तत् वै महा-मोहनम् इन्द्रियाणाम् मिथ्या-अर्थ-योगे अस्य गतिः हि नित्या मिथ्या-अर्थ-योग-अभिहत-अन्तरात्मा स्मरन् उपास्ते विषयान् समन्तात्

words.meaning: his inner self struck by union with false objects

translations.text: That (going) of the senses (to objects) is a great delusion; for in union with false objects his course (in saṃsāra) is constant. His inner self struck by union with false objects, remembering (them), he attends on objects on every side.

notes: Śaṅkara: the moving of the senses among objects, in one overcome by passion, is a great delusion. That is: when a man holds objects to be unreal, his senses do not move toward them; not moving toward objects, they move toward the inward Self, and delusion ceases. When a man holds objects to be real, his senses have gone out to outward objects, and he does not know directly, as himself, the Supreme Self, real, without a second, inward (‘those whose minds are soiled by contact with women's bodies, blinded by the poison of objects, do not know Brahman’). So the great delusion is moving toward objects again and again (Manu 2.94: desire is never appeased by enjoying desires; like fire with ghee it only grows). Then there is union with false objects, sound and the rest, imagined by ignorance; in that union the embodied one's course, the course of saṃsāra, is constant, fixed. For it is well known that those who move toward objects without knowing the Supreme Self as their own, turned outward, reach animal and other births (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.1.1; and verse 13 below). Why is it constant? His inner self struck, his natural being as Brahman struck, by union with false objects, remembering women and other objects, he attends on them, not on the Supreme Self, on every side.

ete bālān mṛtyave prāpayanti dhīrās tu dhairyeṇa taranti mṛtyum || 11 ||

translations.text: Brooding (on objects) first strikes him; and afterwards desire and anger seize him (and strike him). These bring the childish to death; but the wise cross death by steadfastness.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the verse: what follows from that? Hear what happens there.

Śaṅkara: abhidhyā, brooding on objects, first strikes him, makes him fall from his own nature. Then, near the objects, desire quickly seizes him, struck by brooding, and strikes him; then anger seizes him, struck by desire, and strikes him. These, brooding and the rest, bring the childish who have come under their power, without discernment, deluded, to death, cast them into it (Kaṭha 2.1.2: the childish follow outward desires and go into the snare of wide death; the wise, knowing deathlessness, do not seek the lasting among things that do not last). But the wise, conquering objects by steadfastness and knowing the Supreme Self as themselves, cross death (Kaṭha 1.3.15: discerning him, one is freed from the mouth of death).

sanskrit.deva:
योऽभिध्यायन्नुत्पतिष्णून्निहन्यादनाचारेणाप्रतिबुध्यमानः ।
स वै मृत्युं मृत्युरिवात्ति भूत्वा ह्येवं विद्वान्योऽभिहन्तीह कामान् ॥ १२ ॥

yo 'bhidhyāyann utpatiṣṇūn nihanyād anācāreṇāpratibudhyamānaḥ |
sa vai mṛtyuṃ mṛtyur ivātti bhūtvā hy evaṃ vidvān yo 'bhihantīha kāmān || 12 ||

grammar.en: past active participle m. nom. sg.

translations.text: He who, reflecting (on their faults), would strike down the things that rise (and fall), by disregard, not heeding them — he, having become (the death of death), eats death as death (eats creatures); for he who knows thus strikes down desires here.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the verse: how do the wise, conquering objects by steadfastness, cross death?

Śaṅkara: abhidhyāyan: thinking of them as impermanent, impure and shot through with pain. utpatiṣṇūn: objects, called ‘rising’ because they rise again and again and fall. nihanyāt: would abandon them. anācāreṇa: by disregard, indifference, as at the sight of something unclean. apratibudhyamānaḥ: not thinking of them again. That man, becoming the death even of death, eats death as death does (a verse: he who withdraws from objects by discernment is known as the death of death; he is the knower, the knower of the Self, the sage). So the knower, (seeing them) as impermanent and the rest, strikes down desires by disregard and the like.

sanskrit.deva:
कामानुसारी पुरुषः कामाननु विनश्यति ।
कामान्व्युदस्य धुनुते यत्किंचित्पुरुषो रजः ॥ १३ ॥
sanskrit.iast:

kāmān vyudasya dhunute yat kiṃcit puruṣo rajaḥ || 13 ||

lines.iast: kāmānusārī puruṣaḥ kāmān anu vinaśyati
kāmān vyudasya dhunute yat kiṃcit puruṣo rajaḥ

padaccheda.iast: kāma-anusārī puruṣaḥ kāmān anu vinaśyati kāmān vyudasya dhunute yat kiṃcit puruṣaḥ rajaḥ
padaccheda.deva: काम-अनुसारी पुरुषः कामान् अनु विनश्यति कामान् व्युदस्य धुनुते यत् किंचित् पुरुषः रजः

translations.text: A man who follows desires perishes after his desires. Casting off desires, a man shakes off whatever dust (of merit and sin) there is.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the verse: but what does he do who does not strike down desires by disregard?

Śaṅkara: he who through brooding on objects follows desires perishes after them: when the object of desire is destroyed, he perishes with the desires; the objects of desire are impermanent, perishing every moment, and the man who desires them withers like them. But he who, seeing the faults of objects, abandons desires, casting them off shakes off, destroys by discerning understanding, whatever dust, action of merit and sin, he has gathered in this birth or another.

sanskrit.deva:
देहोऽप्रकाशो भूतानां नरकोऽयं प्रदृश्यते ।
गृध्यन्त एव धावन्ति गच्छन्तः श्वभ्रमुन्मुखाः ॥ १४ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
deho 'prakāśo bhūtānāṃ narako 'yaṃ pradṛśyate |
gṛdhyanta eva dhāvanti gacchantaḥ śvabhram unmukhāḥ || 14 ||

lines.iast: deho 'prakāśo bhūtānāṃ narako 'yaṃ pradṛśyate
gṛdhyanta eva dhāvanti gacchantaḥ śvabhram unmukhāḥ

padaccheda.deva: देहः अप्रकाशः भूतानाम् नरकः अयम् प्रदृश्यते गृध्यन्तः एव धावन्ति गच्छन्तः श्वभ्रम् उन्मुखाः

translations.text: This body of beings is dark; it is seen to be a hell. Coveting (bodies), they run on, going into a pit with faces upturned.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the verse: how is this body, which is desired, something to be given up?

Śaṅkara: this body of beings that is seen is dark, a dense darkness without a gap, simply a hell, because it is full of phlegm, blood, pus, worms, excrement and urine (Manu 6.76–77: this dwelling of the elements, with bones for posts, bound with sinews, plastered with flesh and blood, covered with skin, foul-smelling, full of urine and faeces, beset by old age and grief, the seat of disease, afflicted, impermanent, should be abandoned). Though the body of a woman and the like is so loathsome, they covet it, thinking it lovely, and run after it. ‘Going into a pit with faces upturned’: as the blind, unable to discern a well and the like, fall into it with faces upturned, so, blinded by the poison of objects, longing for women and the rest, they fall, faces upturned, into hells.

क्रोधाल्लोभान्मोहभयान्तरात्मा स वै मृत्युस्त्वच्छरीरे य एषः ॥ १५ ॥

words.meaning: his inner self (filled) with delusion and fear

translations.text: He who does not think of the other (the Self, beyond objects), O warrior, does not learn (the science of the Self); his (body) is like a tiger made of straw. (Moved) by anger and greed, the inner self (filled) with delusion and fear — that is death, this (self) that is in your body.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the verse: for those who so covet and run on, the body is useless.

Śaṅkara: he who runs after women and the like, blinded by the poison of objects, not knowing the Supreme Self, his own Self, other than these, does not learn, does not take up, the science of the Self that has it for its object. For him, though he knows the Veda with its six limbs, the body is useless, like a tiger made of straw (Vasiṣṭha: a brāhmaṇa who knows the four Vedas but does not find the subtle Brahman is a brāhmaṇa-donkey, weighed down by the load of the Veda). Not only is the body useless: such a man is himself his death. ‘From anger and greed’: from these two as causes, the inner self joined with delusion and fear, this self of yours seen in your body, is your death. He who, his senses unconquered, with anger, greed and the rest, moves among objects is himself his death, for he is the cause of his ruin (Gītā 6.5: the self alone is the friend of the self, the self alone its enemy).
The edition: kaścid anyaṃ as read in the print (the transcript notes that common texts have kaṃcid anyam).

sanskrit.deva:
एवं मृत्युं जायमानं विदित्वा ज्ञानेन तिष्ठन्न बिभेति मृत्योः ।
विनश्यते विषये तस्य मृत्युर्मृत्योर्यथा विषयं प्राप्य मर्त्यः ॥ १६ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
evaṃ mṛtyuṃ jāyamānaṃ viditvā jñānena tiṣṭhan na bibheti mṛtyoḥ |
vinaśyate viṣaye tasya mṛtyur mṛtyor yathā viṣayaṃ prāpya martyaḥ || 16 ||

lines.iast: evaṃ mṛtyuṃ jāyamānaṃ viditvā jñānena tiṣṭhan na bibheti mṛtyoḥ
lines.deva: एवं मृत्युं जायमानं विदित्वा ज्ञानेन तिष्ठन्न बिभेति मृत्योः

lines.iast: vinaśyate viṣaye tasya mṛtyur mṛtyor yathā viṣayaṃ prāpya martyaḥ
lines.deva: विनश्यते विषये तस्य मृत्युर्मृत्योर्यथा विषयं प्राप्य मर्त्यः

padaccheda.deva: एवम् मृत्युम् जायमानम् विदित्वा ज्ञानेन तिष्ठन् न बिभेति मृत्योः विनश्यते विषये तस्य मृत्युः मृत्योः यथा विषयम् प्राप्य मर्त्यः

translations.text: Knowing death thus as it arises, standing in knowledge, one does not fear death. In his range death perishes, as a mortal (perishes) on coming into the range of death.

notes: Śaṅkara, introducing the verse: by what means, then, is death destroyed?

Śaṅkara: knowing thus the death called heedlessness, the seed of every evil, birth, death and the rest, as it arises in the form of anger and the rest, abandoning anger and the other faults that burn beings and gaining freedom from anger and the rest, standing in knowledge, as Brahman, consciousness, being, bliss without a second, one does not fear death (Taittirīya 2.9: knowing the bliss of Brahman, one fears nothing). Why? In the range of that knower, when the Supreme Self is directly realized, the death of ignorance called heedlessness perishes. As a mortal who has come into the range of death, saṃsāra, is overcome by death and destroyed, so the death of ignorance, come into the range of the knower of the Self, is destroyed (the Nāmamahodadhi: he who stands in knowledge, the fire of knowledge, bearing the thunderbolt of knowledge, is known as the slayer of death).

Śaṅkara, closing: so, by ‘when action arises’ (verse 9) and what follows, actions have been shown to be causes of bondage, and by ‘standing in knowledge one does not fear death’ knowledge alone has been shown to be the means of liberation. On this Dhṛtarāṣṭra raises an objection.

sanskrit.deva:
यानेवाहुरिज्यया साधुलोकान्द्विजातीनां पुण्यतमान्सनातनान् ।
तेषां परार्थं कथयन्तीह वेदा एतद्विद्वान्नैति कथं नु कर्म ॥ १७ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
yān evāhur ijyayā sādhulokān dvijātīnāṃ puṇyatamān sanātanān |
teṣāṃ parārthaṃ kathayantīha vedā etad vidvān naiti kathaṃ nu karma || 17 ||

lines.iast: yān evāhur ijyayā sādhulokān dvijātīnāṃ puṇyatamān sanātanān
teṣāṃ parārthaṃ kathayantīha vedā etad vidvān naiti kathaṃ nu karma
lines.deva: तेषां परार्थं कथयन्तीह वेदा एतद्विद्वान्नैति कथं नु कर्म

padaccheda.iast: yān eva āhuḥ ijyayā sādhu-lokān dvijātīnām puṇyatamān sanātanān teṣām para-artham kathayanti iha vedāḥ etat vidvān na eti katham nu karma
padaccheda.deva: यान् एव आहुः इज्यया साधु-लोकान् द्विजातीनाम् पुण्यतमान् सनातनान् तेषाम् पर-अर्थम् कथयन्ति इह वेदाः एतत् विद्वान् न एति कथम् नु कर्म

grammar.en: past active participle m. nom. sg.

translations.text: The worlds of the good that they speak of as (won) by sacrifice, most holy and everlasting, (the worlds) of the twice-born — the Vedas here declare them the highest aim. Knowing this, how is it that the knower does not go to action?

notes: Śaṅkara: how can actions be causes of bondage, when they speak of worlds won by sacrifice, by the Jyotiṣṭoma and the rest: worlds of the good, reached by the righteous, most holy, pure, everlasting? Here, in this round of saṃsāra, the Vedas declare those worlds, up to the world of Brahmā, to be the highest human end. Knowing this, how does the knower not go to action, the means to them, not perform it? Or: how does the knower, the knower of Brahman, not go to action, the means to the worlds up to the world of Brahmā?

sanskrit.deva:
एवं ह्यविद्वान्परियाति तत्र तथार्थजातं च वदन्ति वेदाः ।
स नेहायाति परं परात्मा प्रयाति मार्गेण निहन्त्यमार्गान् ॥ १८ ॥
sanskrit.iast:
evaṃ hy avidvān pariyāti tatra tathārthajātaṃ ca vadanti vedāḥ |
sa nehāyāti paraṃ parātmā prayāti mārgeṇa nihanty amārgān || 18 ||

lines.iast: evaṃ hy avidvān pariyāti tatra tathārthajātaṃ ca vadanti vedāḥ
lines.deva: एवं ह्यविद्वान्परियाति तत्र तथार्थजातं च वदन्ति वेदाः

lines.iast: sa nehāyāti paraṃ parātmā prayāti mārgeṇa nihanty amārgān
lines.deva: स नेहायाति परं परात्मा प्रयाति मार्गेण निहन्त्यमार्गान्

padaccheda.iast: evam hi avidvān pariyāti tatra tathā artha-jātam ca vadanti vedāḥ saḥ na iha āyāti param para-ātmā prayāti mārgeṇa nihanti amārgān
padaccheda.deva: एवम् हि अविद्वान् परियाति तत्र तथा अर्थ-जातम् च वदन्ति वेदाः सः न इह आयाति परम् पर-आत्मा प्रयाति मार्गेण निहन्ति अमार्गान्

grammar.en: past active participle m. nom. sg.

translations.text: Thus the man without knowledge goes about there, and so too the Vedas speak of the range of ends (for him). He (the knower) does not come here: being the supreme Self, he goes to the highest; by the path (of knowledge) he strikes down the wrong paths.

notes: Śaṅkara: true. Thinking thus that the happiness to be won in the world of Brahmā and the rest (is worth having), blinded by the poison of objects, the ignorant man goes about there, in the action that is the means to those worlds; not the knower, for he sees the faults of ignorance and the rest (Bṛhadāraṇyaka 4.4.11: joyless are those worlds, covered by blind darkness; to them, after death, go the ignorant). So too the Vedas speak of the whole range of ends for that same ignorant man. Since they speak of them for the ignorant, not for the knower, the knower does not come here, does not engage in the transient happiness of the world of Brahmā or the action that is its means. What then does he do? Knowing the Supreme Self as himself, being the supreme Self, being Brahman itself, he goes to the highest; and by the path he strikes down the wrong paths, the paths opposed to the Self, causes of saṃsāra, which are dharma, adharma and worship (upāsanā).

Śaṅkara, on another reading, evaṃ hi vidvān pariyāti tatra: the knower of the qualified Brahman reaches there, in the world of Brahmā and the rest, the fruit of his worship, and the Vedas speak of his range of ends: he does not come here, is not born again as the man of rites is, but by the worship of Brahman strikes down the wrong paths; having gone there and struck them down, being the supreme Self, in time he goes to the highest Brahman.

Śaṅkara, summing up: so far it has been shown that the ignorance called heedlessness is death and heedfulness, abiding in one's own nature, deathlessness (verse 4); from ‘from the mouth this death goes forth’ (verse 7) to ‘that is death, this that is in your body’ (verse 15), that this death, turned into its effects, is the cause of every evil; then, asking how it is destroyed, that it is destroyed by knowledge of the Self (verse 16); then the doubt whether the world of Brahmā and the rest are the human end (verse 17), answered by showing that they belong to the ignorant and are no human end (verse 18); and liberation by the path of knowledge was taught in ‘being the supreme Self he goes to the highest’, which states the oneness of the jīva and the Supreme. Not bearing this, Dhṛtarāṣṭra objects.

kiṃ vāsya kāryam athavāsukhaṃ ca tan me vidvan brūhi sarvaṃ yathāvat || 19 ||

lines.deva: किं वास्य कार्यमथवासुखं च तन्मे विद्वन्ब्रूहि सर्वं यथावत्

padaccheda.deva: कः असौ नियुङ्क्ते तम् अजम् पुराणम् सः चेत् इदम् सर्वम् अनुक्रमेण किम् वा अस्य कार्यम् अथवा असुखम् च तत् मे विद्वन् ब्रूहि सर्वम् यथावत्

grammar.en: past active participle m. voc. sg.

translations.text: If he (created) all this in order (and entered it), who is it that directs him, the unborn, the ancient? What is his purpose, or else what unhappiness (is there for him in it)? Tell me all that, O wise one, as it is.

notes: Śaṅkara: if the Supreme Self, marked by truth and the rest, having created in order the world from space to earth, entered it and, standing as the self made of food and the rest, transmigrates, who is it that directs, impels, him, the unborn, the ancient, marked by truth and the rest, in saṃsāra? If it is no other but himself, what purpose has he in moving in many births? Or, if he rests still in his own glory, not moving in births, what unhappiness, what evil, would there be in his entering saṃsāra? Tell me all this as it is. Yājñavalkya, the lotus among the knowers of Brahman, having told the creation of all from him and granted that he himself is the jīva, says the same: ‘if so, how is Brahman born in sinful births? how is the Lord joined with unwanted states?’ By ‘who is it that directs’ Dhṛtarāṣṭra states plainly the quibbler's objection to the view that Brahman is the jīva.
